candidates.title: Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis mimicking progression of interstitial lung disease during treatment for adult-onset still's disease: An autopsy case report.
candidates.abstract:
RATIONALE: Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (sPAP) is a rare disorder caused by impaired surfactant clearance due to alveolar macrophage dysfunction and is often associated with hematologic disorders or immunosuppressive therapy. In patients with connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD), worsening respiratory findings are frequently interpreted as progression of the underlying ILD, which may delay recognition of sPAP, particularly when anti-granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) antibodies are negative. In the present case, preexisting ILD and repeated bronchoscopic findings of organizing pneumonia further obscured the development of sPAP, making the diagnosis particularly challenging.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A 68-year-old woman with adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD)-associated ILD developed progressive respiratory deterioration during immunosuppressive therapy. Despite apparent control of AOSD-related systemic inflammation, serum Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6) levels increased markedly, and new diffuse ground-glass opacities appeared on chest computed tomography.
DIAGNOSES: Repeated bronchoscopic examinations demonstrated organizing pneumonia without features suggestive of PAP, supporting the interpretation of progressive CTD-ILD. However, KL-6 levels progressively increased to 19,333 IU per liter despite treatment, raising suspicion of PAP. Anti-GM-CSF antibody testing was negative, and a definitive diagnosis could not be established during life. Autopsy ultimately revealed sPAP with periodic acid-Schiff-positive intra-alveolar material and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Hematologic abnormalities had initially been attributed to systemic inflammation, and subsequent bone marrow examination showed MDS-like dysplasia without establishing a definitive diagnosis of MDS.

candidates.title: Treg dysregulation in the oxidative lung milieu: an emerging mechanistic link in interstitial lung disease associated with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases.
candidates.abstract: Systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease (SARD-ILD) is a fatal complication, in which the progression of pulmonary fibrosis has been closely linked to immune microenvironment imbalance and oxidative stress. Regulatory T cells (Tregs), as a central component of immune tolerance, play a crucial role in suppressing excessive inflammation. Current evidence suggests that oxidative stress may contribute to Treg dysregulation through several interrelated mechanisms, including redox-sensitive regulation of Foxp3 expression and stability, disruption of IL-2 signaling, and remodeling of the inflammatory microenvironment. However, the majority of the mechanistic evidence is derived from experimental models or related autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, with limited direct validation in patients with SARD-ILD. These proposed interactions may contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle of oxidative stress and Treg dysregulation, potentially promoting effector T-cell activation, fibroblast proliferation, and imbalanced inflammation and repair, thereby contributing to pulmonary fibrotic remodeling. This review integrates current evidence on the potential links among oxidative stress, Treg dysregulation, and pulmonary fibrosis in SARD-ILD, and proposes an emerging mechanistic framework to guide further investigation into their possible interactions and therapeutic implications.
candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionInterstitial lung disease (ILD) comprises a heterogeneous group of inflammatory and fibrotic disorders that primarily affect the pulmonary mesenchyme and represents a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) (1–3). SARD-ILD may occur in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic sclerosis (SSc), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), Sjögren’s disease (SjD), idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM)-including polymyositis, dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome, and immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy-and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) (4, 5). Notably, patients with SSc exhibit a high mortality rate, with a median survival of only 2–3 years in certain cases, thereby imposing a substantial burden on society and families (6). The conventional perspectives attribute pulmonary fibrosis primarily to dysregulated fibroblast activation (7). Accordingly, current clinical treatments primarily aim to inhibit fibroblast activation; however, this approach has shown limited efficacy, serving mainly to delay disease progression rather than reversing fibrosis, with some patients even developing resistance to treatment (8). Recent studies have implicated immune-microenvironment imbalance as a potential contributor to the development of SARD-ILD (9–11). Regulatory T (Treg) cells are essential for maintaining immune tolerance and homeostasis (12), and their functional impairment may be associated with the progression of pulmonary fibrosis. Furthermore, oxidative stress has been implicated in pulmonary fibrotic remodeling. Excessive ROS and RNS may damage cellular macromolecules and promote alveolar epithelial cell apoptosis, macrophage polarization, myofibroblast differentiation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling, thereby contributing to lung injury, inflammation, and fibrosis (13, 14). However, much of this evidence derives from IPF and experimental pulmonary fibrosis models, and its direct relevance to human SARD-ILD remains to be established. Treg homeostasis is also sensitive to metabolic and redox perturbations: ACC1-regulated mitochondrial metabolism influences Treg suppressive function (15), whereas ROS-dependent SOCS3 upregulation can destabilize Tregs in experimental autoimmune settings (16). Taken together, oxidative stress may influence Treg stability through redox-sensitive regulation of Foxp3-associated pathways (16, 17). In parallel, pro-inflammatory macrophage responses may remodel the immune microenvironment (18), whereas context-dependent metabolic cues may modulate Treg homeostasis and suppressive function (19, 20). Collectively, these interacting processes may form a self-reinforcing pathological cycle (16, 21) that disrupts immune homeostasis, promotes excessive effector T cells activation (22, 23), abnormal proliferation of fibroblasts (24), and imbalanced macrophage-mediated inflammation and repair (25), thereby contributing to the progression of pulmonary fibrosis. Given this framework, an in-depth exploration of the molecular mechanisms by which oxidative stress disrupts local pulmonary immune tolerance, alongside a thorough elucidation of the Treg dysfunction in SARD-ILD, holds promise for identifying novel precision therapeutic targets. This narrative review summarizes and critically discusses relevant research advances, with particular attention to the strength, disease context, and translational relevance of the available evidence. Importantly, the collected evidence supporting the relationship among oxidative stress, Treg dysregulation, and pulmonary fibrosis is heterogeneous. Additionally, direct mechanistic evidence from patients with SARD-ILD, particularly from lung tissue or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, remains limited. Since the majority of the mechanistic insights discussed in this review are derived from experimental pulmonary fibrosis models, other autoimmune diseases, or non-pulmonary inflammatory conditions, the findings of this review are considered supportive or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than direct proof of a causal pathway in human SARD-ILD. To maintain conceptual clarity and scientific rigor, we have distinguished direct SARD-ILD evidence from evidence extrapolated from related experimental and disease settings whenever possible. candidates.title: Association of CYFRA 21-1 with quantitative CT-defined fibrotic progression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Although cytokeratin-19 fragment CYFRA 21 - 1 is a potential biomarker for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), its relationship to imaging-based structural progression remains unclear. We evaluated whether baseline CYFRA 21 - 1 is associated with fibrotic progression measured via quantitative computed tomography (QCT) and compared these associations with Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6), including longitudinal relationships between changes in serum biomarker levels and QCT measures.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 95 patients with IPF who underwent volumetric chest CT, serum biomarker analysis including CYFRA 21 - 1 and KL-6, and pulmonary function tests at baseline and approximately 1 year. QCT measurements, including fibrosis, ground-glass opacity (GGO)-reticulation extent, and total interstitial lung disease (ILD) extent, were measured using deep learning-based software.
RESULTS: Baseline CYFRA 21 - 1 was associated with QCT-defined fibrotic progression (odds ratio per 1 ng/mL increase, 1.347; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.007-1.801). Baseline KL-6 was also associated with fibrotic progression (odds ratio per 100 U/mL increase, 1.085; 95% CI, 1.011-1.164), although the strength of association was lower. Longitudinal increases in CYFRA 21 - 1 were associated with progression of QCT-defined fibrosis (β = 0.943; 95% CI, 0.287-1.600), whereas changes in KL-6 were more closely associated with QCT-derived GGO-reticulation extent (β = 0.429; 95% CI, 0.179-0.680). Neither biomarker was associated with pulmonary function-based progression.
CONCLUSIONS: CYFRA 21 - 1 was associated with QCT-defined fibrotic progression in IPF, whereas KL-6 showed stronger associations with GGO-reticulation extent and total ILD extent on CT. These findings suggest complementary imaging-based association patterns of the two serum biomarkers.
candidates.fulltext: IntroductionIdiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing interstitial pneumonia with a median survival of 3–5 years and a survival rate of approximately 20%. Despite advances in antifibrotic therapy, IPF remains highly heterogeneous with varying rates of clinical progression as well as declining lung function and response to treatment [1]. Increased understanding of this heterogeneity has led to a shift toward precision medicine approaches targeting inflammatory and fibrotic pathways [2]. However, reliable tools for accurately monitoring structural disease progression in individual patients remain limited.Krebs von den Lungen-6 (KL-6), a mucin-like glycoprotein secreted by regenerating type II epithelial cells, has been widely studied as a biomarker for disease severity, progression, clinical outcome, and treatment response [3–5]. CYFRA 21 − 1, a circulating fragment of cytokeratin-19 released by damaged epithelial cells, has recently emerged as a potential biomarker predicting disease progression and mortality in longitudinal studies [6]. Although KL-6 is used for routine monitoring in certain Asian countries [5, 7], circulating biomarkers have not yet been adopted in international consensus guidelines due to their limited specificity and insufficient validation [8]. A key limitation of peripheral blood biomarkers is the uncertainty regarding how well they reflect structural and biological processes occurring within the lung.High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is central to the diagnosis and monitoring of IPF. Recent advances in quantitative CT (QCT) analysis enable objective quantification of interstitial lung disease components and detection of structural changes that may not be fully captured by pulmonary function tests [9–11]. QCT assessment of ILD has been increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant imaging outcome associated with 1-year functional changes and transplant-free survival in recent studies, suggesting its potential value for clinical monitoring and therapeutic trials [12, 13].However, it remains unclear whether different circulating biomarkers correspond to distinct radiological characteristics of disease progression. In particular, the relationship between circulating biomarkers and objectively quantified structural progression on CT remains incompletely understood. Integrating circulating biomarkers with imaging-derived structural endpoints may therefore help characterize imaging-based patterns of disease progression in IPF.Accordingly, the primary objective of this study was to evaluate the association between baseline serum CYFRA 21 − 1 levels and fibrotic progression assessed using quantitative CT in patients with IPF, and to compare its prognostic performance with that of KL-6. We hypothesized that CYFRA 21 − 1 and KL-6 would show different associations with QCT-derived structural components of disease progression. candidates.title: Pediatric anti-GBM crescentic glomerulonephritis: partial renal recovery following plasmapheresis and mycophenolate mofetil.
candidates.abstract: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) glomerulonephritis is a rare cause of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in children. The disease is characterized by the formation of antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane, leading to diffuse glomerular injury and rapid deterioration of renal function if not diagnosed and treated promptly. We report the case of a 14 year-old girl who was admitted with acute-onset edema and hypertension. Initial investigations revealed hematuria, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, progressive renal impairment, and positive anti-GBM antibodies. Kidney biopsy confirmed the diagnosis, demonstrating diffuse crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane. The patient was treated with high-dose corticosteroids, plasmapheresis, and mycophenolate mofetil. After three months of treatment, both clinical and laboratory parameters improved, with partial recovery of renal function. This case highlights the importance of early recognition and prompt treatment of pediatric anti-GBM disease and suggests that an MMF-containing combination regimen may be a feasible alternative to cyclophosphamide-based therapy in selected patients.

candidates.title: Laryngeal Manifestations of Rheumatic Disease.
candidates.journal: Rheumatic diseases clinics of North America
candidates.abstract: Rheumatologic diseases are systemic, immune-mediated disorders that frequently involve the larynx, producing manifestations that range from subtle dysphonia to life-threatening airway obstruction. Laryngeal involvement may precede systemic disease, progress despite adequate systemic control, or be the sole presenting feature of active disease. Diagnosis relies on flexible laryngoscopy with disease-specific serology and biopsy when indicated. Corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and biologics such as rituximab form the foundation of medical therapy, while surgery ranges from serial endoscopic dilation to open reconstruction, with many patients requiring repeated procedures. A multidisciplinary approach optimizes airway, voice, and swallowing outcomes.

candidates.title: Transplantation of endothelial progenitor cells attenuates pulmonary fibrosis via IFITM3-containing exosomes.
candidates.abstract: Endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) are critical for vascular regeneration after injury. However, their role in pulmonary fibrosis (PF) remains unclear. Here, we identified a previously unrecognized population of lung capillary EPCs coexpressing c-KIT and FOXF1 (capEPCs) in adult human and mouse lungs. capEPCs were significantly reduced in lungs from patients with PF and in bleomycin-injured mice, implicating loss of this regenerative endothelial population in disease pathogenesis. Transplantation of donor capEPCs attenuated experimental PF, improved survival, reduced collagen deposition, and restored lung function. Donor capEPCs engrafted into the lung microcirculation of bleomycin-injured mice. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 as a highly enriched transcript in capEPCs. Conditioned media from IFITM3-overexpressing EPCs or recombinant IFITM3 enhanced endothelial proliferation and angiogenesis while suppressing TGF-β1-induced fibroblast activation in vitro. IFITM3 was found in capEPC-derived exosomes. Treatment with IFITM3-containing exosomes recapitulated the therapeutic effects of capEPC transplantation by improving endothelial function, inhibiting fibroblast activation, increasing animal survival, reducing lung fibrosis, and restoring lung function. Together these findings identified capEPC deficiency as a feature of PF and demonstrated that IFITM3-containing exosomes promoted vascular repair. Restoration of capEPC regenerative function or delivery of IFITM3-enriched exosomes may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for human PF.

candidates.title: Translational PBPK Modeling and Exposure-Response Analysis of AT-RvD1 for Treating Sjögren's Disease.
candidates.abstract: Sjögren's disease (SD) is an autoimmune condition characterized by chronic inflammation and impaired secretory function of the salivary glands (SG). The proresolving lipid mediator AT-RvD1 restores SG function in SD-like mice; however, its tissue pharmacokinetics, exposure-response relationships, and human dose predictions remain poorly understood. Therefore, this exploratory study characterizes AT-RvD1 tissue pharmacokinetics, develops an SG-focused physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model, explores the relationship between SG exposure and secretory response, and predicts human exposures relevant to clinical development. Following intravenous administration of AT-RvD1 to SD-like mice, concentrations were quantified in serum, submandibular gland (SMG), heart, lung, liver, and kidney. These data were used to evaluate a PBPK model incorporating the SG as the target site of action. PBPK-predicted cumulative SMG exposure was subsequently compared with the saliva flow rate obtained after chronic AT-RvD1 treatment. The mouse model was then used to predict systemic and SG exposure in a virtual human population across an exploratory dose range. The PBPK model described systemic and tissue pharmacokinetics, with average fold error and absolute average fold error values within predefined acceptance criteria. Human PBPK simulations predicted dose-dependent increases in SG exposure and identified 1.5 mg/kg as a candidate dose at which predicted concentrations exceeded the preclinical pharmacological reference concentration in more than 90% of simulated subjects. Collectively, these analyses provide an experimentally informed PBPK framework for exploring AT-RvD1 tissue exposure, exposure-response relationships, and candidate doses for future clinical evaluation in SD.

1IntroductionSjögren's disease (SD) is a chronic autoimmune condition characterized by progressive inflammation and diminished secretory function of the salivary glands (SG), resulting in impaired saliva secretion and debilitating xerostomia [1]. Diagnostic criteria include dry mouth (often caused by hyposalivation), lymphocytic infiltration into the SG and presence of antinuclear autoantibodies in plasma [2]. SD greatly decreases the patient's quality of life [3] and although extensive investigation has been done to understand it [4], the specific causes of and effective treatments for the disease are still poorly understood. Current therapies for hyposalivation are largely symptomatic and include saliva substitutes and secretagogues that provide limited or transient benefit without addressing the underlying inflammatory processes driving SG hypofunction [5]. Given the high degree of need and the limitations of current therapies, development of novel treatments to reduce SG inflammation while restoring function is essential.Resolution of inflammation is an actively regulated process mediated in part by a family of lipid‐based specialized proresolving mediators (SPM) which include resolvins, protectins and their aspirin‐triggered (AT) forms, all of which are comparable in their properties to naturally occurring SPM [6, 7, 8, 9, 10] but resist rapid inactivation by eicosanoid oxidoreductases (EOR) [11, 12]. Among SPM candidates and their AT forms, studies within the SG have largely been focused on AT‐RvD1 in light of its tremendous potential [13, 14]. To this end, our previous studies demonstrated that SG expresses the G protein‐coupled formyl peptide receptor 2 (Fpr2) [15, 16, 17] and that pro‐inflammatory cytokine signaling is blocked when this receptor is activated with AT‐RvD1 [13, 14, 16]. These events in turn promote survival and organization of SG epithelial cells [15, 16], thereby suggesting that activation of Fpr2 with AT‐RvD1 promotes resolution of inflammation and tissue repair in SG epithelium. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that Fpr2 is essential for regulating resolution of SG inflammation. In order to translate these effects toward clinical therapy, we generated a humanized mouse model (i.e., hFPR2 mouse injected with LPS) and demonstrated that systemic treatment with AT‐RvD1 reduces SG inflammation and restores saliva secretion and supports the notion that human FPR2 can be activated by AT‐RvD1 to resolve inflammation in vivo [13]. To further investigate whether activation of Fpr2 could be used as a therapy for SD, we treated NOD/ShiLtJ (SD‐like) mice with AT‐RvD1 with results indicating that this treatment fully preserves secretory functioning, downregulates proinflammatory cytokine expression and promotes activation of proresolving signaling pathways [20, 21] thereby suggesting a remarkable potential of AT‐RvD1 for treating SD.Although our previous work established the therapeutic potential of RvD1 [16] and enabled development of a translational physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model [22], AT‐RvD1 has emerged as a more attractive clinical candidate. Moreover, AT‐RvD1 reduces SG inflammation and restores secretory function in preclinical models of SD, supporting its development as a therapeutic candidate [21, 25, 26]. Consequently, pharmacokinetic and translational predictions derived from RvD1 cannot be assumed to apply to AT‐RvD1. Direct characterization of AT‐RvD1 disposition and pharmacodynamic activity is therefore necessary to support its continued development as a therapeutic candidate for SD. Despite compelling efficacy data, the pharmacokinetic determinants of AT‐RvD1 activity remain poorly understood. Specifically, tissue distribution of AT‐RvD1 to the SG and the relationship between target‐organ exposure and restoration of secretory function have not been established. candidates.title: Parasite-Derived IL-33 Inhibitors Prevent Bleomycin-Induced Lung Fibrosis.
candidates.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive lung-scarring disease in which epithelial injury, consequent release of alarmins such as interleukin (IL)-33, and immune activation contribute to extracellular matrix deposition. The intestinal helminth Heligmosomoides polygyrus bakeri (Hpb) secretes immunomodulators that suppress type 2 immunity, including HpARI2, which binds IL-33, and HpBARI_Hom2, which blocks the IL-33 receptor ST2. Here, we test this parasite-derived dual blockade strategy in the bleomycin (BLM) mouse model, moving from live Hpb infection to administration of total Hpb excretory/secretory products (HES), and finally administering recombinant HpARI2 and HpBARI_Hom2 proteins. Hpb infection and HES treatment prevented BLM-induced lung fibrosis when administered during the early inflammatory phase. Recombinant HpARI2+HpBARI_Hom2 reproduced this protection, reduced collagen deposition and hydroxyproline accumulation, and dampened ILC2, eosinophil, macrophage, and neutrophil responses. In contrast, HES or HpARI2+HpBARI_Hom2 administration failed to reverse established fibrosis when administered later in the model. Similarly, administration of the IL-33trap fusion protein could replicate these effects, suppressing fibrosis when administered in the early inflammatory, but not later fibrotic phases of this model. These findings identify parasite-derived inhibition of the IL-33 axis as a defined molecular mechanism by which helminth products can prevent early inflammatory fibrogenesis, while also demonstrating that IL-33 blockade is unlikely to reverse established lung scarring.

Despite intensive research, the precise mechanisms driving disease initiation and progression remain uncertain. However, environmental and occupational exposures to agents such as silica [2], wood [3], metal dust [4], and cigarette smoke [5] are IPF risk factors. These trigger damage to bronchial and alveolar epithelial cells, which could thereby release alarmin molecules into the extracellular milieu [6].Among the many cellular and molecular players implicated in IPF, IL‐33, a member of the IL‐1 family of cytokines, has emerged as a key mediator linking epithelial injury, immune activation, and fibroblast function during IPF. IL‐33 is constitutively expressed by alveolar type 2 (AT2) epithelial cells in the lung, where it is stored in the nucleus until epithelial damage and necrosis cause its release [7]. Upon release, IL‐33 signals through the ST2 receptor (IL1RL1) and its co‐receptor IL‐1RAcP, activating downstream pathways including NF‐κB and MAPK, which lead to the activation and proliferation of immune cells [8]. In IPF, IL‐33 expression is upregulated in the lungs of asthma, COPD, and IPF patients [9, 10], and elevated IL‐33 levels have been correlated with progressive tissue injury and disease severity [10, 11, 12]. IL‐33 contributes to fibrosis by promoting type 2 immune responses, characterised by increased production of IL‐4, IL‐5, and IL‐13, which favour alternative macrophage activation and eosinophil recruitment, both of which are known to support fibrotic remodelling [11, 13, 14].Targeting the IL‐33/ST2 axis represents a promising approach for intervention in IPF. In mouse models, studies in which the IL‐33 pathway is blocked, either through genetic deletion (e.g., IL‐33 or ST2 knockout mice) or pharmacologic inhibition (e.g., anti‐IL‐33 or anti‐ST2 antibodies administered throughout the model), have consistently shown attenuation of fibrosis when the pathway is blocked from the beginning of the model [11, 15, 16, 17, 18]. These interventions dampen the type 2 immune environment that drives fibrogenesis. However, because these models involve blocking IL‐33 signalling from the outset, it remains unclear whether IL‐33 inhibition is solely preventative or if it can also act therapeutically once fibrosis is established.Addressing this distinction was the goal of the current study. Although approved anti‐fibrotic agents such as Nintedanib [19] and Pirfenidone [20] can slow disease progression, they do not reverse established fibrosis, nor do they target the upstream immune mechanisms contributing to disease initiation and progression. A new approach to fibrosis prevention could be to utilise pathogen‐derived immunomodulation. Helminths provide a biologically distinct route into this question because they have evolved secreted proteins that modulate host alarmin responses. Hpb can suppress liver and skin fibrosis through poorly understood mechanisms [22, 23]. candidates.title: Gut microbiome-driven mechanisms in inflammatory bowel disease-associated interstitial lung disease: from dysbiosis to therapeutic implications.
candidates.journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
candidates.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing immune-mediated disorder of the gastrointestinal tract. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) associated with inflammatory bowel disease has been receiving increasing attention. With advances in the gut-lung axis theory, accumulating epidemiological and mechanistic evidence indicates that the association between IBD and ILD is not coincidental or merely driven by drug toxicity, but rather reflects a systemic disease spectrum involving microbiome dysbiosis and cross-organ immune dialogue. This article presents a critical narrative review that systematically summarizes the mechanisms underlying IBD-related ILD, focusing on causal evidence from large cohort and Mendelian randomization studies. It also looks at how gut microbial metabolites remotely regulate lung immune homeostasis, the inflammatory cascades triggered by gut barrier disruption and bacterial translocation, and the therapeutic potential of microbiome-based interventions. This article examines the main limitations and controversies, including the limited accuracy of animal models, the unclear causal link between microbial changes and disease onset, and the challenges in selecting clinical trial endpoints. It also outlines future research directions, focusing on integrating multi-omics, non-invasive diagnostic models, and strategies to distinguish drug-induced lung injury from primary disease involvement. This review aims to elucidate the pathogenesis of this cross-organ disease spectrum and to provide a theoretical foundation for both basic research and clinical translation.

As one of the most prevalent occupational diseases globally, pneumoconiosis can cause substantial impairment of lung function and impose a sustained economic burden on affected individuals, families, and society. The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study indicates that the global burden of pneumoconiosis remains substantial (2). According to the 2019 GBD study, pneumoconiosis accounted for approximately 900,000 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost globally (3). In China, approximately 1.368 million prevalent cases were reported in 2019, accounting for more than 60% of the global burden (4). Although ongoing improvements in occupational disease surveillance and management have contributed to a decline in the reported number of occupational pneumoconiosis cases in China (5), pneumoconiosis remains without a curative treatment. Its chronic progression may result in long-term reductions in work capacity and quality of life, as well as adverse effects on mental well-being, while imposing substantial socioeconomic costs (6). Therefore, pneumoconiosis remains a major priority for occupational disease prevention and control in China (4).Cardiovascular complications, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and pulmonary heart disease (PHD), are major contributors to disability and mortality among patients with pneumoconiosis (7). Progressive dust-induced lung injury promotes pulmonary vascular remodeling and elevated pulmonary arterial pressure, increasing right ventricular afterload and ultimately leading to PHD, thereby markedly raising mortality risk (8, 9). Clinical studies indicate that over one-third of pneumoconiosis patients with large shadows develop pulmonary hypertension, resulting in right ventricular overload, dilatation, hypertrophy, and progression to PHD (10). Furthermore, epidemiological studies suggest that long-term silica exposure is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, especially PHD (11, 12). However, models specifically developed for PHD risk screening in patients with pneumoconiosis remain scarce. One logistic regression (LR) model incorporating disease duration, pneumoconiosis stage, and the Tei index was developed to assess PHD risk, but its generalizability was limited (15). Another LR model, restricted to silicosis patients, used pulmonary hypertension rather than PHD as the outcome (16). A cohort study identified platelet count and plateletcrit as factors associated with PHD risk but did not develop a risk-prediction tool (17). These studies were conducted at single centers, lacked external validation, and did not employ machine learning approaches beyond conventional LR. Although pulmonary function tests, computed tomography (CT), and echocardiography are well-established approaches for assessing disease severity in pneumoconiosis and PHD, their routine use for population-level risk screening may be constrained by limited accessibility, cost, and the need for specialized personnel and equipment. candidates.abstract: Multiple cavitary lung lesions present a diagnostic challenge, with a broad differential diagnosis, including infectious, malignant, and autoimmune etiologies. ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), particularly in its seronegative form, is a rare yet important cause that is frequently overlooked, as pulmonary involvement is uncommon and its manifestations can closely mimic infection or malignancy. We report a case of a 30-year-old male who presented with a three-week history of dyspnea and hemoptysis, and a background of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis confirmed by renal biopsy three months prior, consistent with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. Chest radiography and contrast-enhanced CT revealed multiple bilateral cavitary lung lesions with air-fluid levels, micronodules, and centrilobular ground-glass opacities. Extensive infectious workup, including sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures, acid-fast bacilli smear, GeneXpert, and fungal studies, was negative. Cytological examination excluded malignancy. Both p-ANCA and c-ANCA were negative. Based on the 2022 ACR/EULAR classification criteria, a diagnosis of ANCA-negative microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) was established, with a total score of +6 derived from imaging findings consistent with interstitial lung disease and histopathological evidence of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis in a prior renal biopsy. Immunosuppressive therapy with methylprednisolone and mycophenolate sodium was initiated, resulting in complete radiological resolution of all cavitary lesions within two months. This case highlights that cavitary lung lesions may represent a rare pulmonary manifestation of ANCA-negative MPA. A negative ANCA result should not exclude vasculitis when clinical suspicion is high, and tissue biopsy remains essential for definitive diagnosis in atypical presentations.

Their clinical value is no longer confined to a single disease setting; rather, they are now incorporated across metastatic, perioperative, and selected adjuvant strategies (4, 5). This expansion has been accompanied by a parallel rise in immune-related adverse events, a group of toxicities that can affect almost any organ system and frequently require treatment interruption, corticosteroid exposure, or multidisciplinary management (6–8). Among these toxicities, Checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP) occupies a distinctive position because it may be uncommon yet clinically consequential, with the potential to cause rapid respiratory deterioration, prolonged immunosuppression, and interruption of otherwise effective anticancer therapy (9–11).CIP is particularly challenging because it does not present as a single, uniform clinicopathologic entity (9, 12, 13). Some patients develop incidentally detected ground-glass opacities with minimal symptoms, whereas others present with hypoxemic respiratory failure and diffuse parenchymal injury (13–15). The clinical course may be abrupt or indolent, self-limited or relapsing, steroid responsive or steroid refractory (16–18). These differences are not merely semantic. They influence the urgency of diagnostic work-up, the threshold for hospitalization, the pace of corticosteroid escalation, and the safety of later immune checkpoint inhibitor rechallenge (19–21). In daily practice, clinicians are often required to make these decisions before the biological nature of the lung injury is fully understood (22, 23).The current diagnostic and therapeutic approach to CIP remains largely anchored to severity grading systems that were designed to standardize adverse event reporting rather than to capture biological heterogeneity (19, 24). CTCAE grading is useful for communication and triage, but it does not fully distinguish inflammatory burden, radiographic extent, dominant immune-cell programs, or the likelihood of corticosteroid response (10, 17, 22, 25).This limitation matters because patients with the same grade may differ substantially in trajectory and management needs (11, 14, 15). A mild-appearing radiographic phenotype may still reflect active immune injury, whereas some severe presentations may already have evolved into diffuse alveolar damage or steroid-resistant inflammation (13, 17, 26). At the same time, the differential diagnosis of CIP is broad and clinically consequential, including infection, radiation pneumonitis, tumor progression, pulmonary embolism, and exacerbation of pre-existing interstitial lung disease (12, 27, 28).Over the past several years, advances in bronchoalveolar lavage, tissue-based profiling, single-cell transcriptomics, and real-world cohort studies have begun to reveal that CIP is immunologically heterogeneous (10, 25, 29, 30). candidates.title: Quantitative Chest CT-derived Fibrosis and Vascular Remodeling and Acute Exacerbation Risk in Mild Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis.
candidates.abstract: Background Acute exacerbations worsen outcomes in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), but the role of vascular remodeling remains unclear. Purpose To determine whether quantitative CT-derived vascular metrics are independently associated with acute exacerbations in mild IPF and whether arterial or venous remodeling mediates the effects of fibrosis burden. Materials and Methods In this retrospective cohort study, patients with mild IPF (forced vital capacity ≥ 80% and diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide ≥ 55%) underwent baseline volumetric high-spatial-resolution unenhanced chest CT between April 2011 and December 2021 at a single tertiary hospital. Fibrosis score (FS) and vascular metrics were assessed using deep learning-based software. The primary outcome was time to acute exacerbation; the secondary outcome was event-free survival for acute exacerbation, lung transplantation, and death (composite outcome). Multivariable Cox models were used to evaluate both outcomes, adjusting for age, smoking status, and pack-years. Mediation analysis was used to assess whether vascular remodeling mediated the association between FS and the outcomes. Results Among 313 patients (mean age, 66.4 years ± 7.1 [SD]; 245 male patients), 86 (27.5%) experienced acute exacerbation, two (0.6%) underwent lung transplantation, and 120 (38.3%) died during a median 6.3 years of follow-up. Higher FS was associated with a higher estimated risk of acute exacerbation (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] range across models, 1.05-1.09; P value range, .001-.10) and of the composite outcome (aHR range, 1.08-1.20; all P ≤ .001). Venous dilatation (aHR, 7.93 [95% CI: 2.56, 24.59]) and venous diameter heterogeneity (aHR, 1.37 [95% CI: 1.16, 1.63]) were associated with increased acute exacerbation risk, whereas higher small-artery volume fraction was associated with reduced risk (aHR, 0.91 [95% CI: 0.86, 0.96]). candidates.title: Variant Class-Specific Phenotypes and Outcomes in Pediatric TBX4-Associated Pulmonary Hypertension.
candidates.abstract:
AIM: To describe the variant class associations with phenotype, natural history, treatment response, and outcomes in children with TBX4-associated pulmonary hypertension (TBX4-PH).
METHODS: Retrospective cohort analysis of children < 18 years referred to the National Paediatric Pulmonary Hypertension Service between 2001 and 2025.
RESULTS: Twenty-one children were identified carrying either a copy number variant (CNV group = 10) encompassing TBX4 or a single nucleotide variant (SNV group = 11). Distinct phenotypic differences were observed between variant classes. Children in the CNV group were referred at a younger age (p = 0.03), more frequently had prolonged oxygen dependence from birth (p < 0.01), more severe lung disease (p < 0.01) and cyanosis (p = 0.04), congenital heart disease (p = 0.03), neurodevelopmental disorders (p < 0.01), and deafness (p = 0.01). Children in the SNV group were less likely to have any lung disease (p = 0.03). Histopathology from five children (CNV = 3, SNV = 2) demonstrated predominantly lung growth abnormalities with variable pulmonary vascular remodeling. Twenty of 21 (95%) children received long-term pulmonary vasodilator therapy, and 9 (43%) received concurrent calcium-channel blockers. Treatment-naïve children (n = 12) demonstrated stable/improved functional class with therapy initiation. Median follow-up was 7.1 years (range 0.7-17.2). Transplant- or Potts shunt-free survival at 1 and 5 years was 100% and 94.4% respectively and was worse in the CNV group (Log-rank p < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: In this large pediatric TBX4-PH cohort, children carrying CNVs had greater multisystem involvement and poorer outcomes than those carrying SNVs, highlighting the importance of the underlying genetic finding for risk stratification and tailored management strategies.
candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionPulmonary hypertension (PH) in children is a heterogeneous condition associated with significant morbidity and mortality, encompassing pulmonary vascular disease occurring in isolation or in association with congenital heart disease, lung disease, developmental disorders and genetic syndromes [1, 2, 3]. Compared with adults, developmental abnormalities of the pulmonary vasculature and lung have a particularly important role in pediatric PH [4]. Advances in genetic testing have increasingly identified monogenic causes that provide insight into these overlapping pulmonary vascular and developmental phenotypes [5, 6]. Rare pathogenic variants in, or deletions of, T‐box transcription factor 4 (TBX4) are now recognized as one of the leading genetic causes of pulmonary hypertension (PH) in children [7, 8, 9]. TBX4 encodes a transcription factor involved in embryogenesis, notably in hind‐limb formation and lung morphogenesis [10, 11]. Microdeletions on chromosome 17q23, encompassing the TBX4 gene locus, were first reported in 7 children, 5 of whom had small patellar syndrome, also known as ischio‐coxo‐podo‐patella syndrome (ICPPS), and 3 of whom also had PH [12]. While this early report involved copy number variants (CNVs) subsequent studies have also identified single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in TBX4 in association with ICPPS, developmental lung disorders and childhood‐onset PH [13, 14, 15, 16, 17], contributing to recognition of a boarder clinical phenotype commonly termed TBX4 syndrome. Other reported features include deafness and congenital cardiac and neurodevelopmental anomalies [12, 13, 14, 17]; however, in individuals with CNVs encompassing TBX4, additional genes within the deleted interval may contribute to these syndromic features.Herein, we describe the largest single‐centre experience of children with TBX4‐assosicated PH (TBX4‐PH), characterizing it's phenotype, natural history, treatment response and outcomes and compare differences between children carrying pathogenic CNVs with those carrying rare deleterious SNVs.2Methods2.1Study Design and PopulationWe conducted a retrospective analysis of all children aged < 18 years with TBX4‐PH referred to the United Kingdom National Paediatric Pulmonary Hypertension Service (NPPHS) from 1st January 2001 to 1st January 2025. Children were included if they had either a pathogenic or likely pathogenic SNV, defined for the purpose of this study as a variant confined to TBX4, including single nucleotide variants, small insertions, deletions or duplications (SNV group), or a pathogenic CNV encompassing TBX4 at chromosome 17q23 (CNV group). All CNVs identified in this cohort were multigene deletions encompassing TBX4. Variant pathogenicity was assigned according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines [18], with incorporation of updated recommendations from the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation Working Group [19, 20]. The requirement for individual informed consent was waived by the NHS Health Research Authority and associated Research Ethics Committee (REC reference17/LO/0008), under the approval titled “Use of routine Great Ormond Street Hospital data for research,” because the study used anonymized routinely collected clinical data.2.2Clinical Assessments and DefinitionsAll children underwent standardized initial assessment, including echocardiography, 6‐minute walk test (when age‐appropriate), and cardiac catheterization with acute vasodilator testing (AVT) using inhaled nitric oxide, where clinically indicated [21, 22]. Acute vasoresponder status was defined by standard criteria [23]. A diagnosis of PH was confirmed by cardiac catheterization, or non‐invasively by multimodal imaging and clinical assessment in children where invasive assessment was not possible. Height, weight, and birthweight were expressed as Z‐scores [24, 25]. Following initial assessment, children were reviewed routinely with clinical assessment and echocardiography at approximately 3‐monthly intervals. Response to pulmonary vasodilator therapy was assessed by change in World Health Organisation functional class (WHO‐FC) at the subsequent follow‐up. Lung disease was defined by the presence of respiratory symptoms or signs excluding dyspnea as a common feature of PH (Table S1), hypoxemia, or requirement for respiratory support. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) was diagnosed according to the European Research Collaboration for Children's Interstitial Lung Disease (ChILD‐EU) criteria, integrating clinical features, chest imaging, multidisciplinary review and lung histology where available [26]. Severity of lung disease was assessed using the ChILD‐EU‐adapted respiratory severity score (RSS), as described by Morgan et al. candidates.title: IFN-γ-Associated Signaling Networks in Interstitial Lung Disease Associated With Sjögren's Disease.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sjögren's disease (SD) is a chronic systemic autoimmune disorder that can affect multiple organ systems. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a clinically significant pulmonary manifestation of SD and is associated with impaired quality of life and increased mortality. Interferon-γ (IFN-γ), a major effector cytokine of Th1 immunity, has been implicated in immune dysregulation and chronic inflammation; however, its contribution to SD-associated ILD (SD-ILD) and its relationship with fibrotic remodeling remain incompletely understood.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This pathway-oriented narrative review synthesized evidence identified through a structured and iterative search of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science, updated through August 2026. Priority was given to direct evidence from SD-ILD. RESULTS: Available evidence supports a conceptual network in which IFN-γ may function as a potential signaling node interacting with JAK/STAT, PI3K/AKT, NF-κB, MAPK, WNT/β-catenin, and IDO-kynurenine-AhR pathways. candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionSjögren's disease (SD) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disorder that principally targets the exocrine glands. Its hallmark clinical features—xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca—arise from progressive dysfunction of the salivary and lacrimal glands, respectively [1]. Beyond exocrine‐gland involvement, SD can affect the lungs, kidneys, liver, and nervous system, underscoring its systemic nature. Pulmonary manifestations, in particular, are recognized as major determinants of morbidity and mortality in these patients [2].Interstitial lung disease (ILD) is the most common pulmonary manifestation of SD, with epidemiologic studies placing its prevalence at 3%–11% [3]. Once ILD develops, quality of life declines sharply; mortality rises to 16% at 5 years, and the 10‐year risk of death is quadrupled [2, 4, 5]. Although SD‐ILD carries major clinical consequences, its pathogenesis remains only partially defined. A prevailing view holds that dysregulated immune‐cell activation, sustained chronic inflammation, and the aberrant expression of multiple inflammatory cytokines converge to fuel pulmonary inflammation and tissue injury; consistent with this concept, studies have documented the aberrant infiltration of T and B lymphocytes into the lung parenchyma [6, 7]. Sustained elevation of tumor necrosis factor‐α (TNF‐α), interleukins (ILs), and other pro‐inflammatory mediators may likewise play a pivotal role in the initiation and progression of SD‐ILD [8, 9].Among the plethora of inflammatory mediators, interferon‐γ (IFN‐γ)—the cardinal effector cytokine of Th1 cells—plays a major role in the immune dysregulation and tissue injury that characterize diverse autoimmune disorders [10]. IFN‐γ is a pleiotropic cytokine that not only underpins antiviral and antitumor immunity but also shapes the trajectory of autoimmune disease by modulating both innate and adaptive immune responses [11]. In patients with SD, elevated circulating IFN‐γ has been reported and associated with higher disease activity [12]. IFN‐γ engages the JAK‐STAT axis to transcriptionally up‐regulate a broad repertoire of pro‐inflammatory genes, thereby fueling immune‐cell activation and tissue infiltration. Concomitantly, it cross‐talks with NF‐κB, MAPK, and other signaling networks to amplify and perpetuate the inflammatory response [10, 11, 12, 13]. Such immunologic and inflammatory derangements have been implicated in lung injury across broader pulmonary inflammatory settings [14].Notably, the role of IFN‐γ in pulmonary fibrosis remains contentious. Early work suggested that the cytokine might exert anti‐fibrotic activity by curbing fibroblast proliferation and dampening collagen synthesis [15]. Emerging evidence suggests that, in certain chronic inflammatory settings, sustained IFN‐γ signaling may contribute indirectly to fibrotic progression by modifying inflammatory and tissue‐repair responses [16, 17].Nevertheless, mechanistic insight into how IFN‐γ governs immune dysregulation, inflammatory escalation, and fibro‐proliferative remodeling in SD‐ILD remains sparse, and a pathway‐level synthesis is still lacking. candidates.title: Antibody-Drug Conjugates in Breast Cancer: Therapeutic-Window Engineering, Tumor Heterogeneity, and Immunotherapy Combinations.
candidates.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have become a major therapeutic class in breast cancer, but their clinical performance cannot be predicted by antigen expression alone. This review uses therapeutic-window engineering as a unifying framework to connect ADC molecular architecture with tumor heterogeneity, clinical positioning, resistance, immune effects, and toxicity. We examine how target selection, antibody properties, linker stability, payload mechanism and membrane permeability, drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR), conjugation homogeneity, and intratumoral delivery jointly determine efficacy and safety. We then distinguish established clinical uses from investigational strategies across HER2-positive, HER2-low/ultralow, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, and triple-negative breast cancer, reflecting the rapid movement of ADCs into earlier treatment lines and selected early-stage settings. Rather than treating ADCs as a homogeneous class, we critically assess how payload class, linker behavior, bystander killing, Fc-mediated activity, and baseline immune context may favor or limit combinations with immune checkpoint inhibitors. We also map resistance along the delivery-to-kill cascade and integrate practical safety considerations, including interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hematologic toxicity, ocular events, and overlapping toxicities in combination regimens. Three principles emerge: ADC efficacy is a systems property; strategies that broaden tumor coverage may also increase normal-tissue exposure; and successful combinations require platform-specific rather than class-wide rationale. Future progress will depend on biomarker-guided sequencing, rational platform selection, and safety-adapted optimization of the therapeutic window.
candidates.fulltext: IntroductionAntibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have evolved from proof-of-concept targeted therapies into a major class of anticancer agents.1–3 Canonical ADCs integrate three core components-an antigen-directed antibody, a chemical linker, and a highly potent cytotoxic payload-to increase tumor-selective drug delivery while limiting systemic exposure.1,2 Following target binding and internalization, ADCs are generally processed through endosomal-lysosomal pathways, leading to intracellular payload release.1,2 For ADCs carrying membrane-permeable payloads, released drug can also diffuse into neighboring antigen-low or antigen-negative cells and generate a bystander effect, an important mechanism for overcoming heterogeneous target expression.1–3 Consequently, the clinical performance of an ADC is determined not simply by cytotoxic potency or target expression, but by how effectively its molecular architecture balances tumor exposure against normal-tissue toxicity-that is, by the engineering of its therapeutic window.1–3In breast cancer, this transition is particularly evident because ADCs are now active across multiple molecular subtypes and increasingly across different lines and stages of treatment.1–4 Sacituzumab govitecan (SG), a TROP2-directed ADC, first established a major role for this drug class in previously treated metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC),5,6 while subsequent Phase III studies have expanded TROP2-directed strategies into hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative disease and other breast cancer settings.4,7 At the same time, the rapid expansion of ADC therapy has exposed important limitations, including heterogeneous target expression, resistance after sequential ADC exposure, and platform-specific toxicities that may restrict dose intensity or treatment duration.1–4,8The HER2 field further illustrates how ADCs have blurred traditional biomarker boundaries. T-DXd demonstrated substantial clinical activity in HER2-low breast cancer, conventionally defined as HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) 1+ or IHC 2+ with negative in situ hybridization, thereby extending HER2-directed treatment beyond conventionally HER2-positive disease.9,10 More recently, the DESTINY-Breast06 trial demonstrated benefit from T-DXd in hormone receptor-positive metastatic breast cancer with HER2-low expression and also supported activity in the exploratory HER2-ultralow population, defined as IHC 0 with detectable membrane staining.11Importantly, low HER2 expression should be distinguished from HER2 heterogeneity. HER2-low and HER2-ultralow describe levels of target expression, whereas HER2 heterogeneity refers to spatial or temporal variation in HER2 expression within a tumor, between tumor regions, or across different lesions.12,13 Such heterogeneity may limit uniform ADC binding and delivery, while membrane-permeable payloads and bystander killing can partially extend cytotoxic activity to neighboring cells with lower or absent target expression.12–15 These observations illustrate a central principle of ADC therapy: target abundance alone is insufficient to determine clinical activity; molecular design and the spatial organization of the tumor jointly shape the effective therapeutic window.1–3Several recent reviews have comprehensively summarized ADC development, molecular design, breast cancer indications, resistance mechanisms, safety, and emerging platforms.4,16–19 However, these dimensions are frequently discussed as parallel topics rather than as interconnected determinants of the same clinical problem. candidates.title: Clinical features and prognosis of EGPA-associated peripheral neuropathy: a multicentre REVEAL cohort study.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Peripheral neuropathy (PN) is a severe manifestation of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA). However, the aetiology of PN in EGPA remains unclear. This study aimed to elucidate the clinical characteristics and prognosis of patients with EGPA with PN using a multicentre database in Japan.
METHODS: Newly diagnosed patients with EGPA between 2006 and 2024 were enrolled in this study. EGPA was diagnosed according to the ACR/EULAR 2022 classification criteria. Initial clinical characteristics were compared between patients with EGPA with and without PN based on BVAS ver. 3.0. The recurrence rate of PN in EGPA patients with neuropathy was also investigated, and risk factors for PN relapse were identified.
RESULTS: Of the 159 patients enrolled in the REVEAL cohort, 107 newly diagnosed and treatment-naïve patients with EGPA were included. MPO-ANCA was positive in 45 patients (42.1%) and 93 patients (86.9%) had PN. The levels of WBC, eosinophil granulocyte, serum immunoglobulin (Ig)G, and serum IgG4 were significantly higher in patients with EGPA with PN than in those without PN. Among them, IgG4 was the most useful clinical indicator for detecting PN in patients with EGPA. Kaplan-Meier estimator showed that 5-year relapse rate of PN among patients with EGPA with PN was 18.6%. The administration rate of intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVCY) was significantly lower in patients with relapse of PN than in those without relapse of PN.
CONCLUSION: Serum IgG4 might be a useful clinical indicator for detecting PN in EGPA and IVCY administration might be effective in preventing PN relapse.

candidates.title: Clinical Characteristics and Outcomes of Patients with Lymphangioleiomyomatosis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare, progressive cystic lung disease that affects women of reproductive age. Although registries from Western countries have provided key insights, comprehensive nationwide data from Asian countries are scarce. This study aimed to characterise the clinical, functional and outcome features of Korean patients with LAM from a nationwide multicentre registry.
METHODS: We analyzed data from patients with LAM enrolled in the Korean Nationwide Rare Interstitial Lung Disease Registry in 2024. Data on clinical and functional characteristics were collected from 20 centers. Longitudinal changes in pulmonary function were assessed using linear mixed-effects models. Individual annual forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) change rates were estimated using linear regression and analyzed to identify associated factors.
RESULTS: Eighty-six women (mean age, 47.3 years) were included; 50% were asymptomatic at diagnosis and 61.6% had complications, including pneumothorax (29.1%) and renal angiomyolipoma (25.6%). Baseline mean forced vital capacity (FVC) and FEV1 were relatively preserved (89.6% and 78.7% predicted, respectively), whereas diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide was mildly reduced (64.3% predicted). Longitudinal analysis revealed no significant overall decline in lung function. However, cough at presentation and higher baseline FEV1 or FVC were independently associated with disease progression. A total of 54.7% of patients received mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors, but no statistically significant differences in the rate of functional decline were observed between users and non-users.
CONCLUSION: This study provides a nationwide characterization of LAM in Korea, showing preserved lung function at diagnosis and frequent mTOR inhibitor use.

candidates.title: Measurement properties of the Canadian occupational performance measure and the pulmonary functional status and dyspnea questionnaire-modified version in interstitial lung disease.
candidates.abstract:

RESEARCH QUESTION: To evaluate the reliability and validity of the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) and the Pulmonary Functional Status and Dyspnea Questionnaire-Modified version (PFSDQ-M) in European Portuguese among people with ILD, and to explore differences between fibrotic and non-fibrotic ILD.
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Cross-sectional study. Internal consistency (Cronbach's α), test-retest/intra-rater and inter-rater reliability assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients [ICC2,1[95%CI]], standard error of measurement (SEM), minimal detectable change at 95% confidence level (MDC95) and Bland-Altman analysis, and floor/ceiling effects were evaluated. Construct validity was explored with correlations: convergent validity with the LCADL, CIS-8, 6MWT and 1-minSTS, only for PFSDQ-M; divergent validity with age and lung function for both instruments. Subgroup analyses compared fibrotic and non-fibrotic ILD.

Propensity score matching (PSM) and multivariate regression models adjusted for baseline differences. Landmark, subgroup, dose-response, and exploratory drug-specific analyses were performed.ResultsAmong 551 patients, 286 (51.9%) received PPIs. After PSM, PPI use was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.08-2.34; p = 0.019), 90-day mortality (HR 1.62, 95% CI 1.15-2.30; p = 0.006), ICU mortality (OR 3.22, 95% CI 1.57-6.59; p = 0.001), and longer ICU stay (β 1.90, 95% CI 0.91-2.88; p < 0.001). candidates.title: Targeting the CD4+ effector memory T cells re-expressing CD45RA suppressor galectin-7: a multi-omics-guided therapeutic strategy for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
candidates.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive interstitial lung disease with limited therapeutic options. Although single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have revealed cellular heterogeneity within the IPF lung microenvironment, the immune drivers with causal relevance remain poorly defined. Here, through large-scale Mendelian randomization integrating multi-omics data, we identified a consistent negative causal association between the proportion of CD4⁺ effector memory T cells re-expressing CD45RA (TEMRA) and IPF risk. Multi-platform validation-including single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and multiplex immunofluorescence-confirmed a significant reduction in CD4⁺ TEMRA frequency in both peripheral blood and lung tissues of IPF patients, establishing this subset as a clinically relevant biomarker. Spatial transcriptomics further revealed a negative correlation between TEMRA differentiation signatures and local fibrotic burden. Mechanistically, integrated single-cell analyses pinpointed metaplastic KRT5⁺ basal cells as a key epithelial population with the capacity to disrupt immune homeostasis. These aberrant epithelial cells upregulate Galectin-7 (LGALS7), which we demonstrate competes with IL-7 for receptor binding, suppresses STAT5 phosphorylation, and limits CD4⁺ TEMRA differentiation, thereby uncovering a previously unrecognized epithelial-immune crosstalk axis in IPF. Guided by these findings, virtual screening of 20,000 compounds identified neoeriocitrin as a Galectin-7 inhibitor that restores STAT5 phosphorylation in vitro and attenuates pulmonary fibrosis in vivo. This study positions Galectin-7 as a druggable target and establishes a novel framework linking epithelial dysfunction to immune dysregulation in IPF.

candidates.title: Pulmonary fibrosis through patients' eyes: an interpretative phenomenological analysis of illness perceptions and acceptance.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive, life-limiting lung disease that causes substantial morbidity. While there is growing recognition of the importance of symptom management and quality of life, little is known about how individuals with IPF perceive their illness, manage emotional responses, and form beliefs about their condition.
OBJECTIVES: The main aim was to explore how people with IPF perceive and anticipate their illness. A secondary aim was to identify key factors-both facilitators and barriers-that affect these perceptions and influence expectations about the healthcare process.
DESIGN: A qualitative approach using interpretive phenomenological analysis (IPA) was employed.
METHODS: Thirty-one semi-structured interviews were conducted with 23 men, and 8 women (mean age 70.4 years, SD = 7.6). Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed according to IPA, facilitating a deeper understanding of how individuals make sense of and reflect on their experiences.
RESULTS: The analysis revealed a complex psychological landscape, shaped by profound emotional struggles, evolving illness representations, and diverse responses to diagnosis. Participants oscillated between suffering (25 individuals, 81%) and acceptance (9 individuals, 29%), conceptual clarity (7 individuals, 23%) and confusion (24 individuals, 77%), resilience and despair. Future outlooks ranged from hopeful anticipation of medical progress (11 individuals, 35%) to a resigned uncertainty (15 individuals, 48%), underscoring the deeply personal and often conflicting ways in which the illness is processed and endured.
CONCLUSION: These findings provide valuable clinical insights to inform more patient-centered care strategies. They also emphasize the need for tailored psychological support to address the emotional complexity of living with IPF.

candidates.title: Research on the role and mechanism of SLC7A5 in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
candidates.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive, chronic and fatal interstitial lung disease. The etiology of IPF remains to be fully elucidated and its prognosis remains poor with a short survival period. Solute carrier family 7 member 5 (SLC7A5) is an amino acid transporter that is responsible for the transportation of large neutral amino acids. The expression of SLC7A5 was found to be significantly upregulated in patients with IPF, as well as in the lung tissues of mice with bleomycin (BLM)‑induced pulmonary fibrosis and in human lung fibroblasts induced by transforming growth factor‑β1 (TGF‑β1). Both SLC7A5 knockdown and the use of the selective SLC7A5 inhibitor JPH203 affected the function of TGF‑β1‑induced myofibroblasts by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. In vivo, JPH203 improved BLM‑induced pulmonary fibrosis in mice by inhibiting the activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. Therefore, SLC7A5 may represent a new therapeutic target for IPF. Future research should focus on therapeutic strategies regulating this target for translation into potential effective treatments for IPF in clinical practice.

candidates.title: Initial Dosage Optimization of Tacrolimus in Connective Tissue Disease-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease Patients: An Exploratory Study.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Tacrolimus has emerged as a promising therapeutic agent for connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD) patients. However, its clinical application is substantially hindered by high interindividual pharmacokinetic variability and a narrow therapeutic window, which poses critical challenges particularly for the formulation of the initial dosage regimen.
METHODS: A retrospective real-world study was conducted on 22 CTD-ILD patients receiving tacrolimus therapy. Comprehensive clinical data were systematically collected, encompassing demographic characteristics, routine physiological and biochemical parameters, and detailed concomitant medication records. A population pharmacokinetic (PPK) model for tacrolimus in CTD-ILD patients was developed using the nonlinear mixed-effects modeling approach implemented in NONMEM software. Monte Carlo simulation was subsequently performed to recommend the optimal initial dosage regimen of tacrolimus for CTD-ILD patients.
RESULTS: Based on the results of the model, we proposed initial dosing regimens: for CTD-ILD patients, the recommended initial tacrolimus dosage was 0.10 mg/kg across the body weight range of 50-100 kg, which yielded a target attainment probability of 89.1-93.5%, a probability below 5 ng/mL was 6.3-10.9%, a probability above 10 ng/mL was 0-0.2%.
CONCLUSION: This was an exploratory single-center PPK analysis recommending the initial dosage of tacrolimus for CTD-ILD patients. We proposed the 0.10 mg/kg regimen as a preliminary model-derived starting dose, which warranted prospective validation and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM). Given the inherent limitations including the relatively small sample size, lack of external validation, further large-scale prospective studies were warranted to confirm these conclusions.

candidates.title: The impact of macrophage metabolism on idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis development and treatment prospectives.
candidates.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrotic interstitial pneumonia of unknown etiology, in which macrophages serve as central orchestrators of the pathological microenvironment. During IPF progression, the alveolar macrophage pool undergoes a critical compositional shift: tissue-resident alveolar macrophages (TR-AMs) are progressively depleted and replaced by monocyte-derived alveolar macrophages (Mo-AMs) harboring a distinct pro-fibrotic transcriptional and metabolic identity. These populations differ fundamentally in their baseline metabolic programs, and both undergo further reprogramming within the fibrotic niche that sustains myofibroblast activation and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. This review systematically examines how metabolic reprogramming across three principal axes (glucose metabolism, lipid metabolism, and amino acid metabolism) drives pro-fibrotic macrophage polarization in IPF. Within each axis, alterations in metabolic flux and intermediate accumulation converge to reinforce the pro-fibrotic phenotype, promote fibroblast activation, and perpetuate ECM deposition. Importantly, these metabolic alterations differ between TR-AM and Mo-AM subpopulations in ways that reflect their distinct ontogenetic origins and predispose Mo-AMs to preferential pro-fibrotic polarization within the fibrotic microenvironment. Building on this mechanistic framework, we systematically categorize pharmacological modulators targeting these metabolic checkpoints and evaluate the integration of advanced drug delivery systems for precision intervention within the alveolar macrophage niche. This review ultimately proposes a therapeutic strategy that co-targets macrophage ontogenetic origin, polarization state, and metabolic reprogramming as an interconnected axis, offering new perspectives for re-educating macrophages to attenuate fibrotic progression in IPF.

candidates.title: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis preceding detection of metastatic oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma after prolonged remission following pembrolizumab therapy.
candidates.abstract: Dermatomyositis is a recognised paraneoplastic inflammatory myopathy although its association with oesophageal malignancy is uncommon. Most reported cases either precede or accompany the initial diagnosis of malignancy. We report a man in his late fifties with previously treated oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma who developed florid dermatomyositis after approximately 6 years of sustained remission following chemotherapy, radiotherapy and pembrolizumab therapy. He presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia and characteristic cutaneous manifestations accompanied by markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-CT demonstrated metastatic oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma involving the thoracic oesophagus, abdominal lymph nodes and liver. Corticosteroids followed by paclitaxel-carboplatin rechallenge chemotherapy resulted in marked improvement in both inflammatory manifestations and tumour burden. The chronology was notable for parallel evolution of inflammatory activity and metastatic disease after prolonged oncological remission.

candidates.title: How extracellular vesicles contribute to pulmonary fibrosis: miRNA-mediated mechanisms, diagnostic potential, and emerging therapeutic strategies.
candidates.abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a progressive interstitial lung disease driven by excessive fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition, for which pirfenidone and nintedanib slow but do not halt disease progression. Extracellular vesicles (EVs)-lipid bilayer-enclosed nanoparticles that shuttle microRNAs (miRNAs), proteins, and lipids between cells-are increasingly recognized as important mediators and potential modulators of fibrotic remodeling. On the pathogenic side, epithelial- and immune-cell-derived EVs can deliver pro-fibrotic miRNAs (e.g., miR-494-3p) that regulate transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β)/Smad and Wnt/β-catenin signaling, promoting fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition and ECM accumulation. Conversely, selected mesenchymal stem cell-derived EV (MSC-EV) preparations have demonstrated anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models through modulation of TGF-β/Smad signaling, M2 macrophage polarization, mitochondrial function, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition; a phase I clinical study has provided initial safety evidence for nebulized administration, although therapeutic efficacy in PF has not yet been established. Beyond MSC-EVs, plant-derived and milk-derived EVs have emerged as potential delivery platforms, although their applications remain largely preclinical. Meanwhile, EVs isolated from plasma, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, sputum, and urine carry disease-associated molecular signatures that may serve as candidate biomarkers for PF detection or monitoring, but require further clinical validation. This review synthesizes recent evidence on the dual roles of EVs in PF pathogenesis and therapy, evaluates their potential diagnostic utility, and discusses translational hurdles-including cargo standardization, targeted delivery, and scalable manufacturing-that must be overcome for clinical adoption.

candidates.title: Smoking exposures and mortality risk in individuals with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a UK Biobank cohort study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Smoking and secondhand smoke (SHS) exposures are established modifiable risk factors for premature mortality, but their joint associations with recorded idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remain uncertain. We examined active and passive smoking exposures in relation to all-cause and cause-specific mortality and evaluated departures from additivity with recorded IPF history.
METHODS: This prospective UK Biobank cohort included 270,644 participants. Exposures comprised baseline smoking status, cumulative pack-years, maternal smoking around birth, adult SHS, and a composite passive SHS indicator. Multivariable Cox models, additive and multiplicative interaction analyses, and restricted cubic spline models were used after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, lifestyle, and genetic covariates.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 13.8 years, 20,959 deaths occurred. Ever-recorded IPF history was associated with all-cause mortality (HR 4.255, 95% CI 3.937-4.597), and active and passive smoking measures were also associated with mortality. In the additive interaction analyses, a positive departure from additivity was observed only between maternal smoking around birth and recorded IPF in relation to respiratory mortality (RERI 16.969, 95% CI 2.935-31.002; AP 0.248, 95% CI 0.082-0.414; SI 1.337, 95% CI 1.068-1.673). Corresponding positive RERI estimates were observed in analyses restricted to White participants, among participants with complete covariate data, and after excluding deaths occurring within the first 2 years of follow-up. The confidence intervals for the other RERI estimates in the primary analysis included zero. Dose-response associations were nonlinear among participants without recorded IPF and approximately linear among those with recorded IPF, although estimates in the latter group were less precise.
